opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the motivation really comes from what long chain-of-thought does to the inference workload.

With reasoning models, the model isn't just reading a long document once. It's *generating* tens of thousands of tokens, sometimes more, in a single trajectory. And during decoding, full softmax attention has to keep a KV cache that grows linearly with sequence length, and every new token has to attend over all of it. So as the reasoning chain gets longer, you're increasingly bottlenecked by memory bandwidth and KV cache size, not by FLOPs. That limits how many sequences you can batch, and it directly affects the cost and speed of RL rollouts too, which matters a lot when you're training these models with reinforcement learning on long trajectories.

Linear attention, or more generally recurrent-style models with a fixed-size state, solve that problem in principle. The state doesn't grow with the sequence, so decoding cost per token stays constant. The catch, which people in the community have known for a while, is that a pure linear model compresses everything into a finite state, so it struggles with precise retrieval: recalling an exact detail from far back in the context. For reasoning, you do sometimes need that. You need to go back and check what you derived earlier, or copy something exactly.

So the hybrid design is a pragmatic compromise. You make most of the layers linear attention, and in our line of work that means something like the delta rule with gating, which is much better than older linear attention at actually managing what's stored in the state, overwriting stale associations instead of just piling them up. Then you keep a small fraction of layers as full attention to handle the precise retrieval. You end up with most of the efficiency benefit, a much smaller KV cache and much higher decoding throughput at long lengths, while the quality on benchmarks, including long-context and reasoning tasks, can match or even beat a full-attention baseline when trained carefully.

I'd also say there was a conviction element. For a long time, linear attention was seen as an academic curiosity that didn't hold up at scale. A big reason I found this direction worthwhile is that the hardware-efficient training algorithms had matured. We can now train these layers with chunkwise parallel kernels that are actually fast on GPUs. Combine that with the fact that long-CoT makes the decoding bottleneck so acute, and it felt like the right moment: the problem had become important enough, and the tools were finally good enough, to make the architecture change worth it at production scale.

r001.rationale: The response describes long reasoning trajectories and their inference costs, but does not identify longer chains of thought as a way to scale inference-time computation to solve more complex problems.

r002.rationale: It says each new token attends over the growing KV cache, which grows linearly with sequence length. This communicates linear attention work per decoding step and, across L generated tokens, quadratic cumulative work.

r003.rationale: It explicitly connects long-CoT decoding bottlenecks to the hybrid design’s efficiency benefits, including a smaller KV cache and higher long-length decoding throughput.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say the honest starting point was a cost problem, not an elegance problem. Once Kimi moved toward long-chain-of-thought reasoning, the models started generating tens of thousands of tokens per answer, and most of that is decoding. With standard full attention, every new token has to read the entire KV cache, so decoding cost and memory grow linearly with the length of the chain. The model isn't getting smarter in that phase, it's just getting more expensive to think.

Linear attention, or more broadly these RNN-style recurrent forms, flips that. The state is fixed size, so each decode step costs the same whether you're at token one thousand or token one hundred thousand. For a reasoning model that's exactly the regime you care about. But pure linear attention has a well-known weakness: it can't do precise retrieval. If the model needs to go back and copy an exact number from step 12 of its own derivation, a compressed fixed-size state will blur that out. Reasoning chains are full of that kind of lookup, so you can't just throw full attention away.

So hybrid is really the pragmatic middle. You keep a small number of full attention layers to handle exact recall and in-context retrieval, and you let the majority of layers be linear or gated-delta style layers that handle the bulk of the sequence modeling cheaply. In our experiments, something like a three-to-one ratio already recovers nearly all of the quality while cutting the KV cache dramatically, and that saving compounds when you're doing RL rollouts at scale, because rollouts are the part of training that's all decoding.

The other thing I'd add is that the linear layers are not just a cheaper substitute. With a decent delta-rule update, they're actually doing something like online learning over the context, and we saw them hold up well on long-context benchmarks, sometimes better than the baseline. So the bet was: you pay almost nothing in accuracy, you get a much flatter cost curve for long reasoning, and you make the RL loop materially cheaper. For a company whose whole thesis is long-horizon reasoning, that trade was pretty hard to turn down.

r001.rationale: The response says long chains of thought lead to tens of thousands of generated tokens and make decoding expensive, but does not explain that longer chains scale inference-time computation to solve more complex problems.

r002.rationale: It states that each new token reads the full KV cache and that decoding cost grows linearly with chain length, but does not explain that cumulative attention work for generating L tokens is quadratic in L.

r003.rationale: It directly says hybrid attention was a pragmatic response to the cost of long reasoning chains, with recurrent layers lowering the cost of decoding them.

astra-6.text:
The motivation was that long-chain-of-thought reasoning makes the cost of attention especially important. As a model reasons for longer, it produces more tokens, and each new token has a growing history to attend to. So the question is: can we make that process more efficient without weakening the model’s ability to use earlier information?

Hybrid attention is an appealing direction because the two kinds of attention have complementary strengths. Linear attention can process long sequences efficiently, while full attention provides direct access to specific details in the history. You can use the efficient mechanism for much of the computation and retain full attention where that access matters.

For reasoning, that balance is worth exploring. A model may need to return to an earlier condition or intermediate result many steps later. We want to preserve that capability while reducing the cost of longer reasoning. The important test is whether those efficiency gains translate into better reasoning under a fixed compute budget.

r001.rationale: The response says longer reasoning produces more tokens, but does not identify longer chains of thought as a way to scale inference-time computation to solve more complex problems.

r002.rationale: It says each new token has a growing history to attend to, but does not explain linear attention work per decoding step or quadratic cumulative work for generating L tokens.

r003.rationale: The response links Kimi’s interest in hybrid attention to reducing the cost of longer reasoning while preserving access to earlier information.

sol-6.1.text:
The motivation was that long-chain-of-thought reasoning changes the economics of attention. As a model thinks for longer, it generates more tokens, and attending over that growing history becomes increasingly expensive. So we wanted to ask: can we make that process more efficient without losing the ability to retrieve something important from earlier in the reasoning?

Hybrid attention seemed like a promising direction because the two types of attention have complementary strengths. Linear attention can process a long sequence efficiently, while full attention provides more direct access to individual tokens. Combining them gives you a way to reduce the cost while preserving that retrieval capability.

For reasoning, the important question is whether those efficiency gains let the model think longer within the same compute budget and still maintain quality. That was the appeal: making longer reasoning practical, while keeping the parts of attention that the model really needs.

r001.rationale: The response says efficiency could let the model think longer within the same compute budget, but does not connect longer chains of thought to scaling inference-time computation to solve more complex problems.

r002.rationale: It says attention over a growing history becomes increasingly expensive, but does not explain the per-step linear growth or the cumulative quadratic work for generating L tokens.

r003.rationale: It identifies reducing the cost of attention as a motivation for making long-chain-of-thought reasoning more practical.
